title: Anatomy and Physiology I
description: Anatomy and Physiology I is the first half of a two-semester human A&P sequence for health and movement disciplines. Students study how molecular, cellular, tissue, and organ-level structures support function and homeostasis, then apply that reasoning to the integumentary, skeletal, muscular, nervous, special-senses, and endocrine systems. Lecture, laboratory, imaging, surface anatomy, measurements, and cases are integrated so students can identify structures, explain mechanisms, interpret normal variation, and recognize introductory departures from normal without drifting into a full pathophysiology course.

topics.title: Course Orientation, Anatomical Terminology, and Homeostasis
topics.description: This opening unit gives students the language and logic of A&P. It teaches how to describe the body precisely, connect structure to function, and explain why physiological systems are organized around stability and feedback.

children.title: Anatomical Position and Directional Terms
children.description: Students learn a shared map of the body so descriptions are precise and unambiguous in lab, clinical notes, and exams.

children.title: Superior, inferior, anterior, posterior, medial, lateral, proximal, distal
Body Planes, Sections, and Cavities
children.description: Planes and cavities help students understand imaging, dissections, organs, and how structures are arranged in three-dimensional space.

children.title: Sagittal, frontal, transverse, and oblique planes
Thoracic, abdominal, pelvic, and abdominopelvic regions
Levels of Structural Organization
children.description: A&P makes more sense when students can move from atoms and cells to tissues, organs, systems, and the whole organism.

children.title: Chemical, cellular, tissue, organ, system, organismal levels
Homeostasis and Feedback Control
children.description: Homeostasis explains why body systems constantly regulate variables such as temperature, calcium, glucose, and blood pressure.

children.title: Negative feedback, positive feedback, and homeostatic imbalance

topics.title: Chemistry for Anatomy and Physiology
topics.description: This unit reviews the chemistry needed to understand cells, tissues, muscle contraction, nerve impulses, and hormone action. The goal is not chemistry for its own sake, but chemistry as the operating system of the body.

children.title: Atoms, Ions, and Chemical Bonds
children.description: Students learn why ions, charges, and bonds matter for membranes, enzymes, muscle contraction, and neural signaling.

children.title: Water, pH, and Buffers
children.description: Water and pH shape nearly every physiological process, from protein structure to blood chemistry and cellular reactions.

children.title: Polarity, cohesion, adhesion, and solvent properties
Acids, bases, pH scale, and buffers
Biomolecules
children.description: Macromolecules are the materials and tools of cells: fuel, membranes, enzymes, receptors, and structural components.

children.title: Chemical Reactions and Energy
children.description: Students see how the body builds, breaks down, and transfers energy in ways that support tissue function.

topics.title: Cells, Membranes, and Cellular Metabolism
topics.description: Cells are the smallest living units students will use to explain tissues and organs. This unit builds fluency with organelles, membranes, transport, protein synthesis, cell division, and energy production.

children.title: Cell Structure and Organelles
children.description: Students learn what cell parts do and how specialized cells reflect the work they perform.

children.title: Ribosomes, rough and smooth ER, Golgi apparatus
Membrane Transport
children.description: Transport explains how cells maintain internal conditions, communicate, and respond to changing environments.

children.title: Protein Synthesis and Gene Expression
children.description: This subtopic connects DNA instructions to the proteins that create cell structure, enzymes, receptors, and tissue function.

children.title: Basic regulation and clinical relevance of protein errors
Cellular Respiration and Cell Division
children.description: Students learn how cells make ATP and renew tissues through controlled growth and division.

children.title: Glycolysis, Krebs cycle, electron transport overview
Cell cycle, mitosis, and basic cancer vocabulary

topics.title: Tissues and Histology
topics.description: This unit teaches students to recognize the four basic tissue types and explain how microscopic organization supports organ function. It also builds lab skills for slide identification.

children.title: Epithelial Tissue
children.description: Epithelia cover surfaces, line cavities, and form glands, so students learn how shape and layering predict function.

children.title: Simple, stratified, pseudostratified, and transitional epithelia
Connective Tissue
children.description: Connective tissues support, bind, protect, store energy, and transport substances throughout the body.

children.title: Cartilage, bone, blood, and adipose tissue
Muscle and Nervous Tissue
children.description: Students preview excitable tissues before studying the muscular and nervous systems in depth.

children.title: Tissue Repair and Membranes
children.description: Repair and membranes connect histology to inflammation, wounds, organ lining, and clinical observation.

children.title: Mucous, serous, cutaneous, and synovial membranes

topics.title: Integumentary System
topics.description: The integumentary system is an accessible system for connecting anatomy, histology, physiology, protection, thermoregulation, sensation, and clinical assessment.

children.title: Skin Layers and Accessory Structures
children.description: Students learn the organization of epidermis, dermis, glands, hair, and nails as a structure-function system.

children.title: Hair follicles, nails, sebaceous glands, sweat glands
Functions of Skin
children.description: Skin is more than a covering: it participates in protection, temperature regulation, sensation, immunity, and vitamin D production.

children.title: Cutaneous sensation and vitamin D synthesis
Pigmentation, Aging, and Repair
children.description: These topics help students interpret visible skin changes and link them to physiology and tissue repair.

children.title: Melanin, carotene, hemoglobin, and skin color
Burns, pressure injuries, and aging changes

topics.title: Bone Tissue and Skeletal Physiology
topics.description: This unit explains bone as a living tissue, not just a rigid frame. Students learn how bone grows, remodels, stores minerals, and responds to mechanical and hormonal signals.

children.title: Bone Cells and Matrix
children.description: Students learn how osteoblasts, osteocytes, and osteoclasts build and remodel mineralized connective tissue.

children.title: Bone Formation and Growth
children.description: Growth explains how the skeleton develops and why age, hormones, and nutrition affect bone structure.

children.title: Calcium Homeostasis and Bone Repair
children.description: Students connect skeletal physiology to blood calcium, fracture healing, and common health concerns.

children.title: Parathyroid hormone, calcitonin, and vitamin D

topics.title: Axial and Appendicular Skeleton
topics.description: This unit focuses on identifying major bones and landmarks while linking skeletal structures to protection, posture, movement, and muscle attachment.

children.title: Axial Skeleton
children.description: The axial skeleton protects the brain, spinal cord, and thoracic organs while establishing the body axis.

children.title: Skull, cranial bones, facial bones, and sinuses
Appendicular Skeleton
children.description: The appendicular skeleton supports limb movement and provides major attachment sites for muscles.

children.title: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
Pelvic girdle and lower limb bones
Hand, wrist, foot, and ankle bones
Bone Landmarks and Lab Identification
children.description: Landmarks matter because nerves, vessels, ligaments, and muscles relate to specific surfaces and projections.

topics.title: Joints and Articulations
topics.description: Joints explain how the skeleton permits movement while preserving stability. This unit prepares students to describe mobility, injury risk, and movement vocabulary.

children.title: Joint Classification
children.description: Students classify joints by structure and function to predict mobility and stability.

children.title: Examples across skull, spine, limbs, and pelvis
Synovial Joint Anatomy
children.description: Synovial joints dominate limb movement, so students learn the components that reduce friction and guide motion.

children.title: Articular cartilage, synovial cavity, synovial membrane
Movement Terminology and Selected Joints
children.description: Movement terms let students describe what muscles do and how joints function in daily activity.

children.title: Shoulder, elbow, hip, knee, ankle, and intervertebral joints
Sprains, dislocations, arthritis, and joint health

topics.title: Skeletal Muscle Tissue and Muscle Physiology
topics.description: This unit explains how skeletal muscle contracts, uses energy, and produces force. It turns memorized muscle names into functional physiology.

children.title: Muscle Fiber Structure
children.description: Students learn the microscopic organization that makes contraction possible.

children.title: Neuromuscular Junction and Excitation-Contraction Coupling
children.description: This subtopic shows how a nerve signal becomes muscle force.

children.title: Muscle Metabolism and Fatigue
children.description: Students connect ATP demand, oxygen use, and fiber type to performance and fatigue.

children.title: Creatine phosphate, anaerobic glycolysis, aerobic respiration
Slow oxidative, fast oxidative-glycolytic, fast glycolytic fibers
Whole-Muscle Mechanics
children.description: Students learn how muscles vary force and produce graded movement.

topics.title: Muscular System Anatomy and Movement
topics.description: This unit builds practical muscle identification and movement analysis. Students learn major muscles by region, action, innervation themes, and functional groupings.

children.title: Naming Muscles and Functional Roles
children.description: Naming patterns help students decode unfamiliar muscle names and predict location or action.

children.title: Direction, size, shape, location, attachments, and action
Axial and Upper Limb Muscles
children.description: Students identify major muscles involved in facial expression, posture, breathing, shoulder motion, and arm movement.

children.title: Head, neck, trunk, and respiratory muscles
Arm, forearm, wrist, and hand muscle groups
Lower Limb Muscles and Movement Analysis
children.description: Lower limb anatomy connects directly to gait, balance, exercise, and injury prevention.

children.title: Hip, thigh, leg, and foot muscle groups
Basic gait, posture, and surface anatomy applications

topics.title: Nervous Tissue and Neural Signaling
topics.description: This unit introduces the language of neural communication. Students learn how neurons and glia support fast signaling, sensation, movement, reflexes, and autonomic control.

children.title: Neurons and Neuroglia
children.description: Students learn the cells of nervous tissue and how structure supports communication and protection.

children.title: Resting Membrane Potential and Action Potentials
children.description: Electrical signaling explains how nerves transmit information across distance.

children.title: Synapses and Neurotransmitters
children.description: Synapses show how neurons communicate with other neurons, muscles, and glands.

children.title: Acetylcholine, norepinephrine, dopamine, serotonin, GABA, glutamate

topics.title: Central Nervous System and Spinal Cord
topics.description: The CNS unit links anatomy to integration: receiving information, interpreting it, coordinating movement, and maintaining consciousness and homeostasis.

children.title: Brain Organization
children.description: Students learn major brain regions and the basic functions associated with each.

children.title: Spinal Cord Anatomy and Reflexes
children.description: The spinal cord integrates sensory input and motor output, including fast protective reflexes.

children.title: Gray and white matter, horns, roots
Reflex arcs and spinal reflex examples
Protection and Circulation of the CNS
children.description: Students learn how the nervous system is protected physically and chemically.

topics.title: Peripheral and Autonomic Nervous Systems
topics.description: This unit shows how the CNS communicates with the body. Students learn cranial nerves, spinal nerves, sensory pathways, somatic motor control, and autonomic regulation.

children.title: Peripheral Nerve Organization
children.description: Students learn how nerves are built and how sensory and motor information travels.

children.title: Somatic Sensory and Motor Pathways
children.description: Somatic pathways connect sensation, voluntary movement, reflexes, and clinical testing.

children.title: Upper versus lower motor neuron themes
Autonomic Nervous System
children.description: Autonomic control explains involuntary regulation of organs, glands, blood vessels, and homeostatic responses.

children.title: Autonomic neurotransmitters and target organ effects

topics.title: Special Senses
topics.description: Special senses connect sensory anatomy to perception. This unit helps students understand how receptors and neural pathways turn stimuli into vision, hearing, balance, taste, and smell.

children.title: Vision
children.description: Students learn how eye anatomy focuses light and how the retina converts light into neural signals.

children.title: Hearing and Equilibrium
children.description: Ear anatomy links sound detection and balance to mechanical and neural events.

children.title: Cochlea, organ of Corti, auditory pathway
Vestibule, semicircular canals, static and dynamic equilibrium
Taste, Smell, and Sensory Integration
children.description: Chemical senses reinforce how receptors detect molecules and contribute to nutrition, safety, and perception.

children.title: Taste buds, papillae, and taste pathways
Adaptation, integration, and clinical changes in sensation

topics.title: Endocrine Foundations and A&P I Integration
topics.description: The final unit introduces endocrine communication and integrates first-semester systems. Students learn how hormones regulate growth, metabolism, stress, reproduction, and mineral balance while revisiting homeostasis.

children.title: Hormone Classes and Signaling
children.description: Students learn how hormones differ from neural signals and how chemical class affects receptor location and response.

children.title: Amino acid-derived, peptide, protein, and steroid hormones
Major Endocrine Glands
children.description: Students identify major glands and connect them to key hormones and regulatory axes.

children.title: Pancreas, gonads, pineal gland, thymus overview
Homeostatic Integration and Lab Synthesis
children.description: This capstone pulls together first-semester systems through applied cases and lab identification.

children.title: Calcium regulation, stress response, and metabolic regulation
Structure-function review across tissues, bones, muscles, nerves, senses, and endocrine organs
Practical lab review using models, histology slides, diagrams, and surface anatomy
